searches.note: Twenty five searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's, and three left unspent. Seven were restricted to a body's or a house's own domain and are read as primary through their summaries: crdobierzo.es once (the four steps of the ladder, the timetable of 2025 and 2030, Merenzao and Estaladiña in the new rules), bodega.raulperez.com once (the range of 2003, the Latin greeting, the making of the 2016), castroventosa.com once (1752, nine generations, Cepas Centenarias since 1999, Mata los Pardos, the field blend), dominiodetares.com once (Dominio Dostares and Prieto Picudo) and losadavinosdefinca.es twice (La Bienquerida; the work from 2017). The rest went to the open web with the author's sources blocked where they would only have repeated themselves (Rare Wine Co, Spanish Wine Lover, Berry Bros., Winetraveler, Skurnik, Bodeboca, Enterwine, Gourmet Hunters by turns). The three shared searches are the denomination's ladder (two) and its recognition of 1989 (one). No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the Consejo Regulador and the houses' own pages for their own dates, vineyards and methods, then to importers and the press for the second source of each date, with the author's sources blocked so that an independent account would show.

Where the sources corrected the record it was set right with its source (the arrival late in the 1990s, the range of 2003, the name of Castro Ventosa in the 1990s, the white grapes of Cepas Centenarias, Prieto Picudo at Dominio Dostares, the serve of Cepas Viejas, Losada's vessels and grapes, La Bienquerida's Vino de Paraje); where a detail rested on one account or none it was cut (the upper limit of the vine, every task by hand, the road through Valtuille's vineyards, little sulphur, bulk wine before 1989, Estaladiña, the work from 2015, unfined and unfiltered on one vintage, El Cepón's plot, the Templar castle in an explanation).

Claims of the house's own dates and vineyards stand, hedged as the house's account where they are its telling. Sources whose title or address names a living person, or that are a writer's own site (a blog, a newsletter, a site named for its writer), were met in the results but never cited; the fragment's sources were changed only where the record now rests on the refuter's, and every new source is listed per record under extraSources.

tested: Founded 1999, the first wine of 1999 and the plots bottled apart in 2001: Polaner Selections, the importer, gives the first vintage 1999 and the separate bottling from 2001 of Las Lamas, Moncerbal, San Martín and La Faraona, and Vinfolio gives La Faraona's first vintage as 2001. Confirmed. One importer's sheet (VVG) gives the house as established in 1998, so the story now says the founders came late in the 1990s and keeps 1999 for the first wine; founded keeps the library's 1999.

The classification: two searches for a rank of the denomination's ladder. The Consejo's own pages (read through search) give the four steps, Viña Clasificada after at least five years as a Vino de Paraje and Gran Viña Clasificada after at least five years as a Viña Clasificada, and foresee the first Viña Clasificada wines no earlier than 2025 and the first Gran Viña Clasificada no earlier than 2030. Merchants call the wine a Gran Viña Clasificada (Bodeboca) and the 2024 a Viña Clasificada (Fine and Rare), but no label or Consejo page read bears either out. Classification stays empty; the trap and the story stand on the Consejo's own words.

The site: the sheets and merchants give a steep plot facing south east on slate and quartzite (the library's holdings say slate and quartzite too) at heights from about 850 to 975 metres. Near the upper limit of the vine rests on no source read and is taken out of the sites, the story, a card and a question; every task by hand rests on none and is taken out.

The making: the house's sheet through its importers gives one oak vat, a share of whole bunches of over three tenths, 45 to 90 days on the skins and 0 to 30 per cent new wood; vintage notes give 26 to 50 days, a foudre of 1,600 litres for some 12 months (2023), 8 months in foudre (2022), 9 and a half months in French barrels (2023, another listing) and 9 to 10 months (2019). Unfined and unfiltered is borne out for 2022 alone and picked by hand by no source read; both are taken out and the time is now eight months to a year.

The ladder: Pétalos del Bierzo, Villa de Corullón and the named sites, Moncerbal, Las Lamas, San Martín (with Fontelas in the village wine), and biodynamic farming are borne out by Polaner and other importers' pages. Confirmed.
The serve (15 to 17 degrees Celsius, a Burgundy glass) sits inside the Codex's range for a medium red; the glass notes agree with the library's and the merchants'.

The house rules: the founders (the son and the nephew) are living and described, never named; the patriarch is described with the house's own name. No price or score: the merchants' scores met in the results are not used. No judging superlative; British; no dash. The questions: one key each, distractors of one kind (four reasons; four pairs of regions), and the explanations teach.

changed.was: The house is named for the descendants of J. Palacios, patriarch of a family of wine growers in Rioja. In 1999 one of his sons, already making wine in Priorat, and that son's nephew came to Bierzo in search of old Mencía on ground hard to reach and slow to yield, and settled on the steep slate around Corullón, on the western edge of the basin. They made their first wine that year. In 2001 they chose to bottle a few plots on their own, and one of them, high near the upper limit of the vine above the village, became La Faraona. Around it the house built a ladder in the Burgundian manner: Pétalos del Bierzo as the regional wine, Villa de Corullón from the village and named sites such as Moncerbal and Las Lamas above it, with the vines farmed biodynamically. The denomination later wrote such a ladder into its own rules, and when it did the Consejo foresaw the first Viña Clasificada wines no earlier than 2025 and the first Gran Viña Clasificada no earlier than 2030. La Faraona shows a sommelier what one high plot of old Mencía can give: perfume and tension rather than weight.

tested: The year of the range: the house's own page (A closer look, read through search) places the first personal project, Ultreia, in 2003; Barberry Garden and Wanderlust Wine give 2003 for the venture apart from the family's estate; VinoNueva and The Happy Vine give 2005 for the company. No source read gives 2004, so the story and the question now say 2003, and founded stays empty.

The trade learnt at the family bodega: several pages give his first vintage at Castro Ventosa in 1994 and the house's page the 1990s as the decade he came to wine. Confirmed; the story says the 1990s.

Ultreia, the Latin greeting of the pilgrims to Santiago: the house's own page says so. Confirmed. The road crossing the village's vineyards: one merchant's summary says the road passes through Valtuille, while the main road runs through Pieros by the hill of Castro Ventosa; it is taken out of the sites, the table and the story, which now say the road crosses Bierzo.

The making: the house's page for the 2016 gives whole stalk fermentation in open oak vats with two to five months on the skins, ageing in barrels and cement, and no fining or filtering; Perrine's gives two to five months; Saratoga Wine gives used barrels and foudres for the 2022 and Empire Wine used barrels of 225 litres for the 2019; the whole bunch share runs from a half to all by listing. The making now says so; old wood is used wood and the truncated cone vats (one listing) are taken out.

The site: the house's page for the 2016 places the wine at Villegas in Valtuille de Abajo, where Gourmet Hunters places Ultreia de Valtuille; the family's vines and several plots each year rest on no source read. The sites now say old vines around Valtuille de Abajo, at Villegas for one vintage.

Others: El Pecado at Amandi in Ribeira Sacra from a small old plot (SommPicks, Vinissimus; one page gives it no denomination, so the trap says where it grows); Sketch an Albariño of Rías Baixas with bottles kept under the sea in the Ría de Arousa (Tecnovino and Vinetur on the experiment from 2010 or 2011, Vinorea on the wine); Ultreia Valtuille a Mencía of the house (its own page). Confirmed.

The denomination of 1989: Wikipedia, ITACyL and the Consejo's own history give the definitive recognition in 1989 after a provisional one of 1988. Confirmed. The serve, 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, sits in the Codex's range for a light red.

The house rules: the grower is never named in prose (the house keeps its name); his nephew and his partner in Sketch, met in the results, are not named. Little sulphur and the opening claim that much of the revival came from such growers rest on no source read and are taken out. The questions: one key each, distractors of one kind (four methods; four Bierzo houses), and the explanations teach.

changed.was: Bierzo was recognised as a denomination in 1989, and much of its revival in the years after came from growers raised among its old vines. The grower behind this house comes from a family of Valtuille de Abajo and learnt his trade at its bodega before going his own way. In 2003, or 2004 by some accounts, he began to bottle under his own name and called the range Ultreia, the Latin greeting pilgrims give one another on the road to Santiago, read as go further. That road runs through the vineyards of the village, and Saint Jacques, the apostle at its end in French, names the Mencía drawn from the family's old vines there, picked from several plots each year. The house works with whole bunches, long macerations, old wood and little sulphur, after perfume and freshness rather than weight. From Bierzo the grower carried the same ways west into Galicia, to Ribeira Sacra and Rías Baixas, so that the house's name is met across the Atlantic north west. Ultreia Saint Jacques is its wide release: the old Mencía of Valtuille, fragrant and lively, made for the table rather than the cellar.
changed.now: Bierzo was recognised as a denomination in 1989, and the grower behind this house comes from a family of Valtuille de Abajo whose bodega is Castro Ventosa. He learnt his trade there in the 1990s before going his own way. In 2003, by the house's own account, he began a range of his own and called it Ultreia, the Latin greeting pilgrims give one another on the road to Santiago, read as go further. That road crosses Bierzo on its way into Galicia, and Saint Jacques, the apostle at its end in French, names the Mencía drawn from old vines around Valtuille. The house works with whole bunches, long macerations in open oak vats and used wood, after perfume and freshness rather than weight. From Bierzo the grower carried the same ways west into Galicia, to Amandi in Ribeira Sacra and to Rías Baixas, so that the house's name is met across the Atlantic north west. Ultreia Saint Jacques is its wide release: the old Mencía of Valtuille, fragrant and lively, made for the table rather than the cellar.
changed.why: The house's own page and two independent pages give 2003 for the first personal range (another account gives 2005 for the company, none read 2004), the road runs through Bierzo rather than demonstrably through the village's vineyards, and little sulphur rests on no source read; the revival claim of the opening rested on none either.

tested: The family since 1752, nine generations, the cellar at the foot of the western slope of the Roman site: the house's own pages (read through search, restricted to castroventosa.com) say so. Confirmed, hedged as the house's account.

The first bottling of 1989 and the name of 1991: Spanish Wine Lover gives the first bottling in 1989 under another family name and the name Castro Ventosa in 1991, as Enterwine does; InfoBierzo, writing for the house's twenty five years, dates the final change to the middle of the 1990s. The story and the question now say the 1990s. Selling in bulk before 1989 rests on no source read and is taken out.

Cepas Centenarias: the house's page gives the first vintage 1999, every vintage bottled since, one plot at Mata los Pardos with vines over a hundred years old, and for the 2021 Mencía with Alicante Bouschet, Bastardo and white grapes and other varieties. Confirmed; the white grapes and the plot's name are added.

The making: Farr Vintners' notes for the 2021 and the importer's sheet give native yeasts in an oak vat, three tenths whole bunches, some sixty days on the skins, a rest of a month or two in tank and a year in used barrels of 225 and 500 litres; another listing calls them French oak. The making now says so; picked by hand (no source read) and unfined and unfiltered (one listing) are taken out.

The hill: the municipality of Cacabelos, Wikipedia and other pages give a walled site by Pieros between Cacabelos and Villafranca, its late Roman wall, the identification with Bergidum Flavium as the accepted one though disputed (La Edrada), and Bierzo's name from Bergidum. Confirmed; the hedges stand. The Templar castle at Ponferrada in an explanation rested on no listed source and is replaced by the house's own word, a Roman site.

The village wine of 2017 for the new ladder: the house's own page for Castro Ventosa Valtuille says so; the denomination's Vino de Villa seal came with the rules ratified in 2019. Valtuille Villegas is labelled Vino de Paraje on the house's own page. El Castro de Valtuille Mencía Joven is the young red (Vinissimus, Indigo Wine, Bodeboca); of the village rests on no source read and is taken out.

The house rules: the family's living members, the grandmother of the first name and the grower of the Ultreia house are described, never named. No price, no score. The questions: one key each, distractors of one kind (four readings of a label term; four sites), and the explanations teach.

tested: Founded in 2000 at San Román de Bembibre: Un Buen Vino, Castilla y León Económica and a press piece on the house's twenty years (2020) give 2000 beside the house's own page. Confirmed. A group of friends and investors as founders is now in two pages, but the record keeps the house's founders as it had them.
Cepas Viejas, the first wine: Un Buen Vino says it was born almost with the house, as the house's own news says. Confirmed.

The vines and soil: La Gaceta Viajera, quoting the house's sheet for the 2022, gives Mencía alone from vines of some eighty five years on slate up to 700 metres in Bierzo Alto; Monlacata and Vino-vi give vines of sixty and more on clay and slate; Noticias del Vino lists clay, limestone, slate and schist. The sites now give sixty to more than eighty years and clay beside the slate; the card no longer fixes the age; the question's chalk distractor, too near a soil one listing gives, is now volcanic ash.

The making: ten months in French oak and about eighteen months in bottle for the 2022 by the house's sheet; nine months in French and American barrels (Vinissimus) and nine to twelve (Monlacata) for others. The making's nine to ten months in oak barrels and many months in bottle stand.
The serve: the house's sheet for the 2022 gives 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; the record's 16 to 17 is now 15 to 16, inside both the house's range and the Codex's for a medium red.

Prieto Picudo and Estaladiña: the house's own page gives Prieto Picudo to its sister bodega, Dominio Dostares, in Los Oteros of León, where it works old vines it has recovered; no source read ties the house to Estaladiña, so that claim is taken out. The Consejo's pages give Merenzao and Estaladiña added in the new rules and the Ministry's approval of 2019; the work from 2015 rests on no source read and is taken out.

The house rules: a person interviewed for the house, met in the results, is not named. Scores met in the results (a guide's points) are not used. The questions: one key each, distractors of one kind (four soils; four villages), and the explanations teach.

changed.was: Dominio de Tares was born in 2000 at San Román de Bembibre, in Bierzo Alto on the eastern side of the basin, as a house set on recovering old vineyards. Its founders, by the house's account, searched the denomination for sites on very different soils. Cepas Viejas was its first wine: a modern red, aged in oak, in which Mencía was meant to stand at the centre, made from bush vines of eighty years and more on decomposed slate. Beside it the house made a Godello fermented in barrel, and it took part in reviving two old reds of the north west, Prieto Picudo of León and Estaladiña of Bierzo. The denomination itself worked from 2015 on new rules that the Ministry ratified in 2019, adding Estaladiña and Merenzao to its grapes and a ladder of village, site and classified vineyard wines. In time the house gave the name Cepas Viejas to its barrel fermented Godello as well, so that a red and a white share it. For a sommelier, Cepas Viejas stands for the Bierzo of the early 2000s: ripe Mencía from old vines, shaped by oak.

Its idea was to recover old vineyards on the clay soils where the valley's growers had long planted Mencía, worked as many small plots rather than one estate. The namesake Losada is drawn from the clay slopes close to the cellar. Above it the range climbs to Altos de Losada, from old plots at Valtuille de Arriba aged in concrete eggs, large casks and barrels, and to La Bienquerida, a single plot of old mixed vines at Las Chas. From 2017, by its own account, the house farmed with cover crops between the rows and replanted with grafted Mencía. Bierzo is often taught through its slate, and Losada is the other half of the lesson. For a sommelier, the namesake wine is the softer side of Mencía: round and generous from clay, beside the taut reds of the slate hills, and an easy first bottle of the valley at the table.

Long dead or undated and described, never named: José Palacios, the patriarch of the house's name (his death in 2000 is in the author's report, his dates not read in two sources); the grandmother whose name the first Castro Ventosa bottling of 1989 carried. The author's Marcos García Alba, of another Valtuille bodega, was not met again.
swapNote: No swap was proposed by the author, and the refuter proposes none. The plan's note on Castro Ventosa asks whether two picks of one family (the bodega and the grower's own range) should stand: they stand, because they are two houses with two wines and the records keep the stories apart (the grower's range of 2003 against the bodega of 1752, 1989 and 1999), each trap telling the candidate which is which. One merchant calls Altos de Losada the house's flagship; the namesake Losada is kept as the wine a guest meets first, and the record claims no rank for it. Descendientes de J. Palacios, Raúl Pérez and Dominio de Tares are real houses of the denomination, each making the wine its record tells, which their own pages and independent accounts bear out.
planNotes: descendientes-j-palacios: the note is answered: no rank of the 2017 ladder is borne out for La Faraona by the Consejo or a label (merchants' Viña Clasificada and Gran Viña Clasificada set against the Consejo's timetable), so classification stays empty. The why stands, save that the house was established in 1998 by one importer's sheet and made its first wine in 1999.

raul-perez: the note is answered: the house prints Ultreia Saint Jacques on its own page and the importer Ultreia St. Jacques, with Bierzo; the record keeps Saint Jacques. The why's consultancy is the library's word, and Barberry Garden calls him the consultant winemaker at the family estate; the why stands.

castro-ventosa: the note is answered: the century old vines are the house's own (vines over a hundred years old at Mata los Pardos), the family vineyards since 1752 are the house's account, and no single founding year holds (1752, 1989, the 1990s). The why's sandy valley floor is not borne out: the house names a plot, not a soil, and one listing gives clay; the why is loose there.

dominio-de-tares: the note is answered: 2000 is borne out by three independent pages; the flagship is the Mencía; the Godello's year of renaming is not settled and is left out. The why's slate and clay is borne out by the listings.

losada: the note is answered: founded stays empty (2005 in most accounts, 2004 in two); the label is Losada with Bierzo on the house's page; La Bienquerida's Vino de Paraje of Las Chas is borne out by the house's own pages, not by a Consejo page.
